content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper introduces a method for style transfer with language labels by using the CLIP space. The training is conducted in 2 stages: first an auto encoder-decoder pre-trained stage, and then a style-specific fine-tuning. For style-specific fine-tuning, the encoder is frozen, and loss relies on the similarity between the CLIP image embedding of the generated image and the CLIP text embedding of the style (and original caption) sentence. Visual results are compared against previous work on style transfer based on language and input images. There is no ablation study or any deep analysis of the components of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strength
* Style transfer based on language clues is an interesting and very recent direction in style transfer.

Weaknesses
* The main problem with the paper is that the visual results are not convincing. Most of the conclusions in the paper are subjective and debatable; for example: "results of StylerDALL-E are much closer [than the previous methods] to artworks of the specific style" (page 8), or "show distinct differences among different styles" (page 8). By looking at the provided examples, I cannot agree with those sentences. To me, the generated images seem less diverse and less similar to the "original style" than the previous work. To avoid this subjectivity, it may help to compute quantitative metrics, for example, diversity of the embeddings of the generated images, and similarity between the generated images and the reference style embedding.
* There is no ablation study or in-depth analysis of the model's components. Are all the proposed parts of the models necessary? How did each of them contribute to the final performance? For example: What happens if there is no pre-training? How affects the down-sampling size? Is the caption really necessary for computing the rewards/loss?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The model description is not very clear. It does not help that the supporting figure (Figure 2) does not include all the components described in the text (e.g. v, e, p). I would suggest to incorporate all the information in the figure, so it is easy to cross-check when reading the text. Also, the fine-tuning needs to be conducted for each style, which I also did not find until I read the experimental section.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes a simple encoder-decoder method for style transfer using text as clues, which is an interesting idea (but not novel, it has already been explored before). Compared to previous work, the method does not seem to produce better-quality images than previous work, which significantly reduces the contribution of the work. If I misunderstood any of the parts of the paper, I am happy to discuss it in the rebuttal period and update my score.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper aims to achieve the task of language-based style transfer. To do so, utilization of a joint visual-language space learned by a pre-trained CLIP model is key. Beyond transferring the target style to the given input image, reducing artifacts and maintaining the content of the input is desired. The paper shows tens of qualitative examples illustrating how the proposed method successfully transfer styles while reducing artifacts and incoherent contents better than the previous work. However, the result is only shown on tens of qualitative examples without more quantifiable evaluation.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
[Strength]

The proposed method is conceptually straightforward and seems reproducible from the clear descriptions in the paper. Ablation studies for proposed components (e.g., captioning or not, scaling or not) are included. Qualitative figures included in the paper verify that the method is successful at least for the shown examples.

[Weakness]

First of all, I do not fully understand the motivation of the task, language-guided style transfer, in several ways:
1) How often are the use cases when one is interested in a specific style that they know its name but doesn't have a reference image for it? It's rather easy to access reference images for most example styles studied in the paper: (a) Monet Impression Sunrise, (b) Picasso cubism, (c) Van Gogh blue color, (d) Van Gogh purple color, (f) ukiyo-e print, (g) fauvism, (h) pixel art illustration, from Fig.3 for example. 
Probably only the style, (e) warm and relaxing, is more abstract/generic and would be better handled by languages than reference images. A visual art dataset collected by [i] provides emotional effects and explanations to artworks in natural languages, including terms like "funny", "bold", "dynamic", "calm and mediative". Reference images for these terms are ill-defined, and I think would be where a language-based style transfer method like this work could be most useful. As a result, evaluation done on this dataset would be more useful and convincing, as opposed to evaluating on art-specific texts like "Monet", "fauvism", "ukiyo-e", pretending reference images for them are not available.
2) This task itself seems ambiguous to me, due to the polymorphism of most texts, and applying to most examples shown in the paper ("oil painting", "watercolor painting", "Van Gogh", "Picasso", "Monet", etc.). Oil paintings and watercolor paintings can come in different brushstrokes, color schemes, and abstractions of the content; artistic styles of the same artist evolve through their different life stages. However, examples of all styles shown in the paper seem to be capturing only one single modality of each artistic style, and there is no mechanism to control which modality of the given artistic style to generate, unless exhaustively describing all properties one can articulate with words (e.g., "low-saturated, watercolor painting, in realism").
3) The key ingredient that allows this method to achieve language-guided style transfer is utilizing CLIP (Radford et al. 2021) space. Doesn't this imply that the proposed method can only transfer styles from seen vocabulary of the pre-trained CLIP model? 

Aside from the motivation, I am currently not fully convinced by the claimed achievements based on the experiment results in the paper, specifically, whether the proposed method "reduces the artifacts and semantic incoherence than previous work" and how well it "captures abstract concepts related to the target style". The comparison with previous work is only shown in qualitative examples, and combining main paper and supplementary file, there are only 12 examples in total. It is unclear how these 12 images were selected; was it randomly selected? Even if it was random, 12 is not a large number. To study whether the proposed method generates less artifacts and more coherent images, a user study on a set of hundreds of randomly sampled images would be supportive. Moreover, since the example styles studied in this paper mostly have reference images (e.g., "Monet", "Van Gogh", "fauvism", etc.), it would be helpful to quantitatively evaluate the style-transfer quality by measuring the similarity of style features between the reference image and the generated image. For example, is it possible to compute the Gram matrices to get style features like the work by Gatys et al. 2016 and compare with baseline methods that do not involve Gram matrices?

[i] Achlioptas, Panos, et al. "Artemis: Affective language for visual art." CVPR 2021.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper is written in a clear way, making it easy for readers to follow and possibly reproduce the results. The quality of the paper is fair, as it builds on concepts from several state-of-the-art work (e.g., non-autoregressive language translation from Gu et al. 2018, DALL-E from Ramesh et al. 2021, CLIP from Radford et al. 2021), and includes tens of qualitative examples to help readers understand how successful the proposed method is. Language-based artistic style transfer using CLIP space has been studied by previous work (Kwon and Ye, 2022), and its main difference to this work is that the previous work requires an additional content loss and thus the need to tune multiple terms in the final loss function. However, the claimed improvement of the proposed method over the previous work is only shown in several qualitative examples. It would be helpful to compare them on a larger scale.
content.summary_of_the_review: The proposed method is shown to be effective in achieving the goal of language-based style transfer given the several qualitative examples in the paper. However, I am not clear about the motivation of when one needs to perform style transfer by texts and not reference images, especially for the example styles (e.g., "Monet", "fauvism", "oil painting", etc.) studied in the paper. Maybe transferring more abstract or generic styles like emotions or feelings (e.g., warm, relaxing, disturbing, etc.) would be more useful for this task? Also, a larger-scale and quantifiable evaluation would be more convincing. Currently, I could only tell that the method is successful and possibly better than the previous work on the selected examples in the paper. How successful this method works beyond these examples is uncertain to me. Elaboration of the above points are in my previous comments in the Strength And Weakness section.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 3: You are fairly confident in your assessment. It is possible that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work. Math/other details were not carefully checked.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper introduces a language-guided style transfer method which uses the latent spaces of
DALL-E and CLIP to inject visual-language semantics in the style transfer. Specifically, a non-autoregressive token sequence translation is used to manipulate the discrete latent space of DALL-E to train an image auto encoder. During inference, the style of reference sentence is injected with cosine similarity in the CLIP space with the concatenated content and style description. A RL approach is used to include a CLIP based reward in the fine-tuning stage.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
+ can transfer abstract style concepts implicitly represented in feature space which cannot
be easily represented using reference images.
+ leveraging pre-trained DALL-E and CLIP models with no large-scale model training

- visual quality not great, with poor texture details compared with reference image-based method
- hard to evaluate the quality and generalization ability of the results given a style description
- inference may be slow with fine-tuning for each query style, a time complexity analysis should be given
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: Most part of this paper is easy to follow, with lots of detailed discussion on implementation. However, a clearer version of high-level architecture of Fig 2 can make the apprehension smoother. With the code promised to be released, reproducing it should not be a problem. The general idea of using language to drive image stylization is not totally new, and we have seen similar ideas in editing images by comparing prompt in CLIP feature space. The biggest question is the low visual quality of stylization results shown in the paper. The current results show the idea can somehow work but not at the quality for practical applications.
content.summary_of_the_review: This paper proposed an interesting design of CLIP space optimization with RL. However, the visual quality is not satisfactory, and the evaluation is hard to judge objectively. Currently, it is hard to draw decisive conclusion from results. With more recent text to image generative models, the results may improve accordingly.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.details_of_ethics_concerns: Bias from pre-trained generative model may bring ethic issues to the results.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This work proposes a language guided style transfer method called StylerDALL-E to achieve image style adjustment through text prompts. It leverages the powerful latent space of existing text embedding models to capture abstract concepts of style. Meanwhile, the style transfer task is formulated as a token sequence translation process. Experimental results on different domains of content images show the effectiveness of the proposed method.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
+ It casts the image style transfer as a problem of visual token translation inspired by language translation
+ It supports style transfer without using a reference style image which might be not at hand

I have a few concerns listed below:

First, language guided image manipulation (including manipulating artistic style) has shown more impressive results in works like StyleCLIP [1], StyleGAN-NADA[2], and VQGAN+CLIP [3]. Though it is subjective to evaluate the visual quality, I personally am not quite impressed by those results for example in Figure 1, which indicates that it didn’t show the obvious advantage of using latent space of DALL-E. Results in this work are still mostly about transferring color and texture while stroke is also a sort of local textures. The higher concept of style should be at least including some geometric change (like those portrait paintings of Picasso), which is already possible to be achieved by abovementioned works. 

[1] StyleCLIP: Text-Driven Manipulation of StyleGAN Imagery
[2] StyleGAN-NADA: CLIP-Guided Domain Adaptation of Image Generators
[3] A Fast Text-Driven Approach for Generating Artistic Content

Though this work claims to focus on artistic style, I do not see why it is limited to artistic style only. In some reference based image artistic style papers which uses gram matrix loss because they find gram works for artistic painting specifically well (e.g., not working for photorealistic style). But for this work, since the language can be either famous painting, or abstract art, or season change, or tone style or anything, I think it is good to level up this work to more generalized image factor manipulation and explore what type of language embedding is most effective and what direction in latent space to achieve slider like manipulation, instead of just a one-click function.

Evaluation is also another big issue. Looks there are only visual results with a few painting styles shown throughout the paper. It is hard to know how robust the proposed method will be with different style prompts. It is suggested to taka a detailed look at previous works about how to conduct quantitative evaluations. Simply for example describing that the results of proposed method have less artifact is a bit unconvincing.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: This work is presented clearly and organized well. Novelty-wise, language driven transfer setting is not a new task but this work explored DALLE latent space and formulate the task as a token translation problem that looks original. I feel it is reproducible upon author's release of some key components.
content.summary_of_the_review: My major concern is that I do not see the obvious advantage of proposed method over previous works under the similar setting. Authors miss the comparison with a major category of works in the experimental part. See the weaknesses.
